arc: PROPOSED. Deepen the bounded choices already used earlier into reproducible procedures, retained samples, distributions and feedback. The learner makes small, useful operations beside the existing museum encounters; the full artifact, its input and its presentation remain named supplied parts. These teaching connections need approval and implementation before any promise of transporting learner work between halls.

halls.title: Keep a generated arrangement
halls.storyboard: At the paired colour grids, the student chooses an arrangement worth recovering. Bringing RGB colours, lists, loops and bounded random choice, they make a colour recipe with a local seeded generator and explicit request order. A proposed adapter would send their colour list to one existing grid while the other holds a witness; this interface is not yet verified. The displays, replay controls and generator internals are supplied. One unused request reveals why a seed alone cannot identify a picture. They keep recipe and seed together, gaining a reproducible construction for later reuse.
halls.storyboard_short: Use paired colour grids. Reuse RGB lists, loops and bounded draws. Teach a local seeded recipe with explicit request order; insert an unused request to change the picture. Supply displays, replay controls and generator internals. Carry recipe plus seed. Open: verify the proposed colour-list adapter and witness grid; promise neither existing transfer nor cross-version replay.
halls.carries: A repeatable recipe and its seed
halls.review_note: Propose a colour-list adapter for one existing grid, retaining the other as witness. Its implementation and available interface still require verification; do not promise cross-version replay.

halls.title: Count what the arrangement loses
halls.storyboard: The ledger's tiles change neighbours when sorted, while their counts and entropy reading stay fixed. Bringing retained lists and seeded samples, the student makes a frequency table from a small symbol record, copies that list before sorting, and displays both arrangements beside the same counts. Copying preserves a snapshot instead of another reference to changing data. The ledger, tile renderer and entropy calculation are supplied. They learn what counting discards and carry both a sample-to-count operation and a way to keep earlier states, without making the statistical reading a measure of freedom.
halls.storyboard_short: Use the ledger's sorting tiles. Reuse retained seeded samples. Teach frequency counting and copying before sorting; compare changed neighbours against unchanged counts and entropy. Supply ledger, tiles and entropy calculation. Carry a snapshot and separate frequency account; entropy does not measure freedom. Open: Definition's colour-record transfer is proposed; the ledger owns its sample.
halls.carries: A copied sample and its separate frequency account
halls.review_note: The current ledger owns its sample; transferring Definition's colour record would be a new connection.

halls.title: Choose who can be chosen
halls.storyboard: At the amber removal board and paired sampling hoppers, the student predicts an impossible choice before drawing. With grid addresses, conditions and a seeded generator, they construct an eligible list, draw one member, and decide whether to return it or remove it before the next draw. The board, hopper animation and removal floor are supplied. This makes sampling with and without replacement usable rather than merely named. The remaining list travels forward as a way to control opportunity; the floor separately shows when removing a visual also withdraws collision.
halls.storyboard_short: Use the amber board, sampling hoppers and removal floor. Reuse addresses, conditions and seeded draws. Teach an eligible list; predict excluded choices, then draw with or without replacement. Supply displays, animation and floor. Carry candidate list and removal policy; distinguish visual removal from lost collision. Open: choose the board adapter or a compact supplied display.
halls.carries: An explicit candidate list and removal policy
halls.review_note: Choose whether learner results drive the board or a compact supplied display beside it.

halls.title: Give each choice a mark
halls.storyboard: The student follows diagonals from the printing screen into the slab arrangement. They bring grid traversal, lines and bounded choices, then construct a small tile drawing in which each retained draw selects one of two diagonal endpoints. Changing the threshold changes the choices; changing the mark changes their reading. The existing screen, wall-scale display and separate navigation study are supplied. They leave with a reusable rule for assigning marks to addresses, knowing that a convincing maze image has not yet established a connected route or a passage wide enough for a body.
halls.storyboard_short: Use printing screen and slab arrangement. Reuse grid traversal, lines and retained draws. Teach mapping each draw to two diagonal endpoints; vary threshold or mark separately. Supply screen, large display and navigation study. Carry an address-to-mark rule. Distinguish the screen's sine-driven bias from fixed learner probability; maze appearance proves neither connected routes nor bodily clearance.
halls.carries: A two-mark generator with explicit threshold
halls.review_note: Keep the screen's sine-driven bias distinct from the fixed-probability learner construction.

halls.title: Let an outcome continue an instruction
halls.storyboard: After throwing the physical die, the student follows the continuing die's chain: six permits another throw, while another face ends the sum. Bringing state, retained outcomes and counting, they make a bounded accumulator called once by each supplied landing event. It records the face, adds its value and decides whether the chain remains open. The die physics, landing-event connection and column display are supplied. They gain a reusable event-driven accumulator without having to implement asynchronous input. A visible limit reports an unfinished chain; the retained sequence distinguishes the total from how it was reached.
halls.storyboard_short: Use physical and continuing dice: six continues, another face ends the sum. Reuse state, sums and retained outcomes. Teach a bounded accumulator invoked once per accepted landing; report unfinished chains at the limit. Supply physics, landing connection and columns. Carry sequence, total and stopping rule. Preserve physically read faces; no RNG substitution, waiting loop or fair-release claim.
halls.carries: A bounded outcome accumulator with a clear stopping rule
halls.review_note: The supplied landing event invokes the learner's accumulator once per accepted throw. Do not replace the physically read face with an RNG, spin a loop waiting for it, or imply fair releases.

halls.title: Separate an increment from a position
halls.storyboard: The turning cube and prism stacks keep their places while their orientations accumulate small changes. Bringing transformations, time steps and random draws, the student makes a short orientation history for one supplied piece, comparing assigning a fresh angle with adding an increment to the existing angle. The stack renderer and its existing controls are supplied. They learn to identify the state that persists and what RESET actually restores, then carry that distinction into a walking position. The wear rig remains a useful counterexample: its changing appearance does not require random input.
halls.storyboard_short: Use turning stacks and wear rig. Reuse transforms, time steps and draws. Compare fresh-angle assignment with accumulated in-plane increments; record orientation and inspect RESET. Supply stack renderer and controls. Carry persistent state versus increment into Walk. Identify the production update's frame dependence; the historical XYZ title misleads, and the wear rig changes without randomness.
halls.carries: A named accumulated state and a separate increment
halls.review_note: Historical map title and old tutorial suggest independent XYZ rolls; current encounter is accumulated in-plane rotation. Its frame-dependent production update should be identified, not copied as a timing model.

halls.title: Build a walk that remembers its position
halls.storyboard: At the terrarium and paired rails, the student predicts a destination before the animation moves there. They bring vector addition, accumulated state and Trace's retained list, then make a walker that adds a sampled displacement to its current position and records each accepted endpoint. The moving bead, timing controls and boundary comparison are supplied. They choose and explain a boundary rule rather than hiding it inside a helper. The resulting walk and record are reusable separately: smooth travel can be supplied, and the trail need not influence the next decision.
halls.storyboard_short: Use terrarium and paired rails. Reuse vector addition, accumulated state and Trace's list. Teach sampled displacements and recorded endpoints; predict a step and state its boundary rule. Supply bead, timing and boundary comparison. Carry walker and separate record; smooth travel need not affect decisions, nor trails guide them. Open: choose a reduced boundary example before full folding.
halls.carries: A walker plus a separate endpoint record
halls.review_note: Choose a reduced boundary example before expanding to the terrarium's full folding implementation.

halls.title: Keep the values before drawing the bars
halls.storyboard: The sampling cabinet gathers falling beads into bars, then redraws those bars without taking new samples. Bringing retained lists and frequency counts, the student constructs a histogram from a saved numerical sample and changes its interval boundaries while retaining every value. Uniform and Gaussian sampling functions, the cabinet and falling-bead animation are supplied, with their input and output ranges stated. The learner distinguishes sampling, clipping and binning, and leaves with a reusable distribution display. A familiar bell shape becomes something to investigate, rather than the expected destination of every random process.
halls.storyboard_short: Use the bead cabinet. Reuse retained samples and counts. Teach numerical bins; redraw boundaries without resampling. Supply uniform/Gaussian samplers with stated ranges, cabinet and animation. Carry a reusable histogram; separate sampling law, finite sample, clipping and binning. Treat the bell shape as a question. Defer sampler mathematics; decide whether an optional derivation follows.
halls.carries: A histogram that can rebin retained values
halls.review_note: Decide whether a later optional lesson derives a sampler; transformation mathematics is supplied here.

halls.title: Make a population with a declared vocabulary
halls.storyboard: The specimen bed, arrival wardrobe and garment comparison show several ways a recipe can admit differences. Bringing generated forms, transformations and sampling, the student makes a small population description: template identity, position and scale are stored separately, then passed to supplied specimen builders. They can preserve a placement while changing the permitted repertoire, or keep the repertoire while changing its distribution. The bed display, specimen geometry and wardrobe interfaces are supplied. The reusable outcome is a population recipe whose discrete kinds and continuous variations remain visible, including changes it cannot express.
halls.storyboard_short: Use specimen bed, wardrobe and garment comparison. Reuse generated forms, transforms and sampling. Teach separate template, position and scale records; vary repertoire independently from distribution. Supply specimen builders, bed and wardrobe interfaces. Carry a population recipe with visible discrete kinds, continuous variation and limits. Open: select the smallest honest builder interface; follow the fourteen-map sequence.
halls.carries: A population description with explicit repertoire
halls.review_note: Current intent retains an obsolete shortened route; use the fourteen-map sequence order. Choose which specimen builder offers the smallest honest interface.

halls.title: Read neighbouring samples
halls.storyboard: The WHITE NOISE and PERLIN NOISE grids let the student compare three neighbouring heights before naming a landscape. They bring grid addresses, seeded draws and value-to-height mapping, then build one short sampled profile using independent draws and another using a supplied coherent field function at the same coordinates. The comparison bench and Perlin sampler are supplied. They measure adjacent differences and change coordinate spacing deliberately, gaining a way to study spatial relationships. A field's correlation is not stored history, and matching displays does not establish matching numerical distributions.
halls.storyboard_short: Use WHITE NOISE and PERLIN NOISE grids. Reuse addresses, seeded draws and height mapping. Teach matched profiles from independent draws and a coherent field; measure adjacent differences and vary coordinate spacing. Supply bench and Perlin sampler. Carry spatial comparison; correlation is not memory, and matching displays do not establish matching distributions. Open: verify perlin_noise_bridge's reduced interface.
halls.carries: A matched profile sampler and neighbour comparison
halls.review_note: Current final centres perlin_noise_bridge, absent from the sequence's older artifact list; verify its reduced interface before writing the tutorial.

halls.title: Give chance a numerical job
halls.storyboard: Among the floor painting, pipes and particle study, the student stops at the dartboard to make an estimate. Bringing coordinates, random sampling, conditions and counts, they construct a bounded point experiment: sample inside a square, test distance from its centre, retain the hit count and compare successive estimates. The dartboard, plotting surface and controls are supplied. They learn why a random draw can support a numerical estimate and carry a reusable sample-test-count procedure. The surrounding works let them compare that purpose with choosing a mark or extending a path.
halls.storyboard_short: Use the dartboard among paintings, pipes and particles. Reuse coordinates, sampling, conditions and counts. Teach a bounded square-sampling experiment: test centre distance, count hits and compare successive estimates. Supply dartboard, plotting and controls. Carry sample-test-count estimation; contrast its numerical purpose with marks or paths. Keep finite-sample error visible: extra draws need not improve each estimate.
halls.carries: A sample-test-count estimator
halls.review_note: Keep finite-sample error visible; more draws need not improve every individual estimate.

halls.title: Let the trace enter the next choice
halls.storyboard: At the terrain console, a visited patch rises while later walkers may return to its fading signal. The student brings a random walker, grid addresses and stored values, then gives their walker a separate signal field: deposit at an address, decay the field, and compare neighbouring values before selecting a step. The terrain renderer, stepped clock and walker display are supplied. They learn feedback by making a trace influence future action. The reusable field remains distinct from accumulated height, and reinforcement supplies no proof that the resulting route is shortest or best.
halls.storyboard_short: Use terrain console. Reuse walker, grid addresses and stored values. Teach a separate signal field: deposit, decay, read neighbours, choose a step. Supply terrain renderer, stepped clock and walker display. Carry feedback into future choices; distinguish fading signal from accumulated height, without optimal-route claims. Open: reusing the learner's walker is proposed; current artifacts own separate states.
halls.carries: A deposit-decay-read field
halls.review_note: Using the student's earlier walker here is a proposed teaching connection; current artifacts own separate states.

halls.title: Compose a finite field from contributions
halls.storyboard: At the noise mixer, broad features remain while finer ones arrive as layers are added. Bringing sine functions, loops and the previous field comparison, the student makes a short weighted sum that samples the same supplied base function at several coordinate scales. They retain each contribution before adding it, so removal and recombination have an inspectable meaning. The mixer display and base sampler are supplied. The outcome is a reusable finite field recipe with separate frequency and amplitude choices, preparing Noise without confusing the sine-based construction with geological processes or stored visits.
halls.storyboard_short: Use the noise mixer. Reuse sine, loops and field sampling. Teach a finite weighted sum across coordinate scales; retain contributions for removal and recombination. Supply base sampler and mixer display. Carry a field recipe separating frequency from amplitude into Noise. Disclose the mixer's display rescaling; distinguish this sine-based construction from geology or stored visits.
halls.carries: A finite field recipe with inspectable terms
halls.review_note: The existing mixer rescales its picture; a teaching display must disclose that mapping while comparing amplitudes.

halls.title: Distinguish a decision from its disclosure
halls.storyboard: The three-stone crossing and door timing trials let the student compare a wait already drawn with one still to come. They bring state, elapsed time and seeded choices, then describe a small event schedule that draws a duration once, stores its deadline and reports its remaining time. The crossing, door trials and collision timing are supplied. This deepens their ability to explain a running process without rebuilding the obstacle course. They carry a reusable distinction between state order, decision time and disclosure, while deciding how much information their own future interaction should expose.
halls.storyboard_short: Use crossing and door timing trials. Reuse state, elapsed time and seeded choices. Teach drawing one duration, storing its deadline and reporting remaining time. Supply crossing, trials and collision timing. Carry a readable schedule separating state order, decision and disclosure; choose what a future interaction reveals. Open: existing-process trace or executable teaching adapter.
halls.carries: A readable schedule of states and decisions
halls.review_note: Choose whether the small schedule is a readable trace of the existing crossing or an executable teaching adapter.

arc: PROPOSED. Follow sampled values into constraints, colours, displacement, occupancy and borrowed coordinates. Reuse the learner's functions and arrays while supplying the field generator itself. Separate correlation from memory and the visible surface from collision. Any shared learner dataset or cross-hall transport below is a proposal; the existing instruments generally own independent samples.

halls.title: Give a candidate permission to remain
halls.storyboard: The held point returns to its plane, while the neighbouring slab keeps only candidates far enough from earlier points. Bringing coordinates, conditions and bounded draws, the student constructs a small placement function that proposes a position, checks its distances from the accepted list, and either records or rejects it. The grabbable point, slab display and proposal counter are supplied. They learn the difference between admission during construction and a constraint enforced every update. Their reusable sampler reports its attempt budget honestly, because failing to place a point does not prove no placement exists.
halls.storyboard_short: Use the constrained point and placement slab. Reuse coordinates, distances, conditions and draws. Teach proposing, distance-checking and accepting/rejecting positions against a retained list. Supply point, slab and attempt counter. Carry a budgeted sampler; failed attempts do not prove impossibility. Distinguish admission from enforcement every update. Defer spectral/audio galleries to comparisons unless separately approved.
halls.carries: A finite placement sampler with accepted and rejected records
halls.review_note: Leave the spectral and audio galleries as comparisons unless a separate lesson is approved.

halls.title: Choose what receives a changing value
halls.storyboard: The three columns share a shaft recipe but receive held, periodic and field-derived values. Bringing sine, elapsed time and generated geometry, the student writes a driver function that returns one scalar and an explicit receiving function that turns that scalar into a column setting. They compare the same recipient under two drivers before changing the recipient. The column builder, local clock controls and marble material are supplied. The reusable outcome is a clean separation of source and use; the independently pulsing orb demonstrates why pausing this clock need not pause the museum.
halls.storyboard_short: Use three columns and independently pulsing orb. Reuse sine, elapsed time and generated geometry. Teach scalar driver and explicit shaft receiver; compare two drivers before changing the recipient. Supply column builder, local clock and marble. Carry source/use separation; stopping one clock need not stop the museum. Follow the actual shaft driver, without invented vertex erosion or loading.
halls.carries: A scalar driver connected to an explicit receiver
halls.review_note: Use the actual scalar shaft driver; do not invent per-vertex Perlin erosion or structural loading.

halls.title: Give one value two visible consequences
halls.storyboard: The paired rings receive the same field as relief and colour. Bringing scalar drivers, mesh positions and colour mapping, the student makes two receiving functions for a retained signed sample: one offsets a position, the other remaps the value into a colour range. The ring mesh, paired probes and noise sampler are supplied. They discover why clipping all negative values to black conceals differences that relief still shows. Their reusable pair of mappings can dress other generated forms, while the layered basin extends the comparison without claiming its different resources are identical octaves.
halls.storyboard_short: Use paired relief/colour rings and layered basin. Reuse scalar drivers, positions and colour mapping. Teach two receivers for one retained signed sample; compare offset geometry with remapped colour and inspect negative-value clipping. Supply ring construction, probes and sampler. Carry reusable mappings. Open: select directly referenced vertices; the basin's different resources are not identical octaves.
halls.carries: Two explicit mappings from one retained value
halls.review_note: Select a small set of directly referenced ring vertices; the full ring constructor stays supplied.

halls.title: Turn a field into occupied cells
halls.storyboard: At the small voxel body and its enlarged counterpart, the student holds one sample steady while the threshold removes its block. They bring multidimensional arrays, field values and conditions, then construct an occupancy array from a supplied field using an explicit height bias and threshold. The cell renderer, section screen and large collision receiver are supplied. The resulting binary volume can be inspected independently of its display. They learn that a visual cut need not change stored occupancy, and that connected occupied cells do not by themselves establish a usable route for a particular body.
halls.storyboard_short: Use small voxel body and enlarged receiver. Reuse arrays, fields and conditions. Teach occupancy from explicit height bias and threshold; hold a sample while changing its classification. Supply cells, section screen and collision receiver. Carry binary volume separate from display. Display cuts need not alter occupancy; connected cells cannot certify access. Open: choose smaller array and receiver.
halls.carries: A stored binary volume separate from its display
halls.review_note: The full 24-cubed volume is supplied; choose a smaller learner array and a disclosed receiver before implementation.

halls.title: Read a surface without mistaking it for support
halls.storyboard: Inside the pink enclosure, the student freezes the material and removes its finish while keeping the doors and floor in view. Bringing layered field sums, colour mappings and the garment's texture-sampling shader, they compose a signed-value-to-colour rule and compare it with the cloud material on the existing panel. The shader host, cloud sampler and room collision are supplied. This deepens the earlier surface lesson before the dedicated shader sequence. They carry a clear account of which operation changes appearance and which could change geometry; a visible fold need not become a place to stand.
halls.storyboard_short: Use the pink enclosure; freeze its finish. Reuse layered fields, colour mappings and Ribbon_Patterns_03's sampler. Teach signed-value colour mapping against the cloud material. Supply shader host, cloud sampler and room collision. Carry appearance/support distinctions; visible folds need not bear weight. Keep this 2D field distinct from Noise_Voxel's volume; dedicated Shaders deepens the supplied setup later.
halls.carries: A declared material mapping and its limits
halls.review_note: Reuses Ribbon_Patterns_03's texture-sampling shader before the later shader sequence deepens it. This hall's 2D field is not Noise_Voxel's stored volume.

halls.title: Change the address before asking for a value
halls.storyboard: Inside the enclosing sphere, the student watches a marked direction remain fixed while its colour changes under WARP. Bringing coordinates, functions and field sampling, they construct two explicit steps: turn a position p into a borrowed address q, then ask the same supplied field for its value at q. The paired images, coordinate witnesses and sphere receivers are supplied. They can inspect the address change before applying colour or relief, gaining a reusable domain-warp function. The floor and pinned doorway edges clarify which parts of the environment receive the deformation.
halls.storyboard_short: Use enclosing sphere and fixed direction witness. Reuse coordinates, functions and sampling. Teach p-to-q address transformation before querying the same field; inspect addresses before colour or relief. Supply offset fields, paired images, witnesses, receivers and collision reconstruction. Carry domain warping separate from receiving. Preserve fixed floor and doorway edges; the study is static between actions.
halls.carries: An address-transform function separate from the field receiver
halls.review_note: Keep the supplied offset fields and collision reconstruction visible as dependencies; this study is static between actions.

halls.title: Test a proposed route against ground
halls.storyboard: The gold proposal and pink walking record cross the same terrain, but only one records a visitor's passage. Bringing Trace's position list, height sampling and surface construction, the student samples a chosen line across the supplied terrain and makes a small height profile to compare with an actual walk. The terrain collision, supported player tracking and recording interface are supplied. They learn to distinguish a geometric proposal from a tested route and carry a reusable terrain-section tool. A second body scale makes clear why a line's continuity cannot certify bodily access.
halls.storyboard_short: Use gold proposal and pink walking record. Reuse Trace positions, height sampling and surfaces. Teach sampling a chosen line through the actual triangle-height query; compare its profile with a walk at another body scale. Supply terrain collision, player tracking and recording. Carry profile and separate passage record; continuity cannot certify access. Open: cross-hall export remains proposed.
halls.carries: A sampled route profile with a separate walk record
halls.review_note: Expose the actual triangle-height query; exporting the student's profile or walk to another hall is proposed.

halls.title: Ask two fields the same question
halls.storyboard: Between the paired cube displays and walk-through arches, the student follows one shared sample address. They bring seeded field recipes and explicit receivers, then make a comparison function that asks two supplied generators for values at the same positions and records their difference. Seed, coordinate scale and output mapping become stated conditions. The Perlin and OpenSimplex2 implementations, arches and sample markers are supplied. The reusable result is a fairer comparison procedure, not a verdict that one field is more natural; removing relief also reveals how much of each arch was authored before sampling.
halls.storyboard_short: Use paired cubes and arches. Reuse seeded fields and explicit receivers. Teach matched addresses and recorded differences with declared seed, scale and output mapping. Supply Perlin/OpenSimplex2 generators, arches and markers. Remove relief to inspect authored arch geometry. Carry comparison conditions into Shaders; preserve correlation versus stored state, without ranking one field as more natural.
halls.carries: A paired field sampler with declared conditions
halls.review_note: Earlier prose sends this directly to CA; the current spine inserts Shaders. Preserve the distinction between spatial correlation and stored state.

halls.title: Keep an unfinished question
halls.storyboard: The optional corridor's dark sphere continues pulsing while the student recalls one change from the Noise halls. They bring a concrete encounter and the operation they traced, then make two short accounts of it: what happened to their view or movement, and which values, addresses or receivers changed. The corridor and sphere are supplied; no new code is required. Choosing a small return experiment leaves them with a useful comparison question rather than a compulsory conclusion. This paragraph is a proposed optional reflection, because the current museum portal does not connect this room.
halls.storyboard_short: Use optional dark-sphere corridor as a proposed reflection; its museum portal is inactive. Reuse one Noise encounter and source/receiver distinctions. Describe both felt view or movement and changed values, addresses or receivers; choose a return experiment. Supply corridor and sphere. Carry a specific unfinished comparison question. Require no new code or compulsory conclusion.
halls.carries: One specific question to test on return
halls.review_note: Listed in noise.json, but intent says dropped from museum and portal is inactive. Do not present it as an implemented route.

arc: PROPOSED. Familiar forms acquire new ways of appearing. Deepen the garment studio’s first shader use: construct a form from a coordinate rule, transform and repeat it, compare its material on different primitive bodies, then alter it with a layered field. Compose these choices before asking what an image must retain to evolve. Keep the existing images → bodies → rooms route. The learner carries a small form function and its settings; museum bindings and transport remain proposed until implemented.

halls.title: Give a familiar form a surface rule
halls.storyboard: At the graph panels, the student returns to the point, distance and the boundary of a face. Bringing coordinates, functions, colour mapping and the garment studio’s first shader, they make one circular mark from distance to a chosen centre. A threshold turns that distance into an inside and an outside; a narrow transition softens the visible edge. The existing graphs explain the rule. The panel, material binding and coordinate display are supplied. The student changes centre and radius independently, then explains why the mark moved while the panel did not. They carry a small mask function and its parameters. A band or box is a later variation; the timed graph remains a comparison, not a second opening lesson.
halls.storyboard_short: Use graph panels to explain a circular mark. Reuse point distance, functions, colour mapping and garment UVs. Teach coordinate → distance → mask; expose centre/radius and compare sharp/soft edge. Supply panel/material binding. Check: move centre without changing radius; explain unchanged mesh. Carry mask + settings. Optional band/box; defer clock analysis. Open: learner binding; softened edge needs valid bounds.
brings: Ribbon_Patterns_03: supplied UVs and sampled material
halls.carries: One small mask function, declared UV frame, centre, radius and edge width
supplied: named material binding and UV display
halls.review_note: The existing hall displays graphs. The learner mask and its host connection are proposed; the deferred Shapes sources provide the operation, not an installed new station. Keep one main form. Use step for a hard edge and ordered, distinct smoothstep bounds for softness. Verify the actual phase-speed control before expanding the clock comparison.
halls.independent_check: Choose another centre without changing the radius. Predict the mark’s position and explain why neither the panel mesh nor its collision moved.
halls.critical_question: Which decision turns a difference in distance into an inside and an outside?

halls.title: Transform the form inside its address
halls.storyboard: The tiled squares return to the earlier floor and garment, where a pattern already depended on how it was sampled. The student brings the retained mask, transforms and array addresses. They first offset and turn a band or asymmetric version of the mark around a named centre, then repeat it in a four-by-four study. The integer tile address chooses a variation; the fractional coordinate evaluates the form inside that tile. One chosen tile turns while the rest keep their orientation. They carry the mask, coordinate transform and address rule as separate parts. The garden offers a further comparison: its supplied world projection lets a pattern cross several bodies. Moving the learner’s function there needs an explicit adapter that preserves that projection.
halls.storyboard_short: Use tiled panels; return to floor/garment sampling. Reuse mask, transforms and array addresses. Offset/turn an asymmetric mark, then repeat 4×4. Teach floor = tile ID; fract = local coordinate. Check: turn one tile only. Carry mask + transform + address rule. Supply host; garden projection stays world-based. Open: binding/transfer adapter. Deferral: no new Shapes/Matrices halls.

array addresses and earlier floor/garment sampling

MODE/RESET rebuild materials; a future adapter must reconnect.

halls.title: Let one material meet different bodies
halls.storyboard: The black ring catches a rainbow rim while the larger primitive bodies answer the lamps. The student returns to the faceted sphere, the garment’s curved receiver and the distinction between moving an object and moving around it. They compare one proposed teaching material on a sphere and a cube before adding a rim from supplied normal and view vectors in the same frame. Dot products now become an appearance. Keeping the material fixed, they change the body or viewpoint and account for the difference. They carry a material whose receiver matters. The existing leather, plastic and oil-like appearances remain available for looking and interpretation; the lesson does not require rebuilding all of them.
halls.storyboard_short: Use ring and staged primitives. Reuse faceted sphere, curved garment, transforms, dot product and retained material. Compare one material on sphere/cube; teach rim from unit normal/view vectors in one frame. Check: predict changed rim with body/viewpoint changed and material fixed. Carry receiver-aware material. Supply geometry/vectors/lamps. Open: shared-material and hold controls absent; emission is not a lamp.
brings: dot products and a retained material
learns: surface normals and view vectors in a common frame

halls.review_note: The hall already supports several primitive body types, but does not provide a shared learner material switch or rotation-hold controls. Those are proposed adapter work. Preserve material associations as interpretation; do not claim simulated fibres, physical optics or a light cast on other bodies by EMISSION alone.
halls.independent_check: Hold the material settings fixed. Predict which rim will change when the camera moves or the receiver changes from sphere to cube, and distinguish that change from the lamp highlight.
halls.critical_question: What makes a computed surface read as softness, leather, display or desire?

tutorial_references.title: Godot 4.6 — Spatial shaders
tutorial_references.purpose: Check the actual normal/view frame and material outputs in the Godot host.

halls.title: Let a field enter the form
halls.storyboard: The student crosses the glass above the moving basin, then returns to the noise panels with the form function they have kept. Noise and weighted sums are familiar; here a finite shader loop combines a few scales with separate frequency and amplitude updates. A bounded contribution disturbs the mask’s boundary while the panel mesh stays fixed. Compare no disturbance with the chosen amount before adding time. The student changes the finest contribution while retaining the broad form and explains the difference. They carry a field function and its range. The basin’s vertex displacement and normal construction are supplied comparisons: its surface moves, but the glass is what carries the visitor.
halls.storyboard_short: Use noise panels and glass-covered basin. Reuse mask, weighted sums and Noise. Teach bounded octave loop; keep frequency/amplitude separate. Perturb mask boundary; compare zero contribution before adding time. Check: change fine detail while retaining broad form. Carry field + range. Supply base noise/material host and basin displacement/normals. Glass supplies support. Defer vertex teaching; coordinate warp optional.
learns: finite octave accumulation in the shader
bounded field contribution to a mask boundary
halls.carries: A finite layered field that can alter the retained form’s appearance
supplied: base noise function and material host
basin mesh, displacement, normals and independent support
halls.review_note: The retained mask-to-field connection is proposed. The mask changes fragment colour, not mesh geometry; coordinate warping is optional. Keep water’s vertex displacement supplied. More octaves do not guarantee visible improvement and do add work; choose a bounded count suitable for the material.
halls.independent_check: Change the contribution of a fine noise scale while keeping the broad mark and its centre recognizable. Identify whether the edit changed colour, sampling coordinates or mesh vertices.
halls.critical_question: Which construction makes the moving surface visible, and which makes the crossing possible?

halls.title: Compose a body and its appearance
halls.storyboard: Among the pink water, sagging sphere and plural body, the student chooses an arrangement worth keeping. They bring the form, repetition, rim and layered field developed here, together with Melencolia’s earlier work of composition. Choosing a supplied body, they combine a limited set of those operations and record what each contributes. One alternate version keeps the geometry but changes its appearance. They distinguish whole-object transformation, supplied vertex deformation and fragment colour. The outcome is a material recipe with reasons for its choices, not a new compulsory technique. The room’s associations remain open: which setting is a default, and who gets to call its appearance excessive?
halls.storyboard_short: Use pink water, sagging sphere and plural body. Reuse Melencolia composition + retained form, repetition, rim and field. Compose limited known effects on supplied body; record choices. Check: make an alternate appearance with geometry fixed; distinguish transform/vertex/fragment. Carry material recipe. Supply lamps/geometry/deformation. Open: composition binding absent. No new compulsory syntax; pink alone is not a theory of queerness.
brings: retained mask, pattern, rim and field
learns: deliberate composition and comparison with known operations
halls.carries: An editable material recipe, receiver choice and an alternate version
halls.review_note: A material-composition adapter remains proposed. The existing unfolding controls do not implement that task. This room can build judgment with known tools; do not impose another algorithm or treat pink as sufficient queer content.
halls.independent_check: Make two appearances for the same geometry. State the few changed inputs and the effect each was meant to produce; account for what the existing lighting still contributes.
halls.critical_question: Who gets to call an appearance excessive, and how did the chosen defaults acquire that meaning?

tutorial_references.title: The Book of Shaders — Shapes
tutorial_references.purpose: Return to a form already owned by the learner.

tutorial_references.title: The Book of Shaders — Patterns
