halls.title: Ask what the form must remember
halls.storyboard: The green panel asks for a previous texture it does not receive. Beside it, branching frost looks grown without retaining that growth. The student brings the form recomputed from coordinates, Paint’s retained image and earlier old-state/new-state updates. They trace which inputs produce each picture, then sketch what would have to be stored for a changed mark to affect the next update. Restarting a clock and restoring a saved state become different operations. They carry this explicit state contract into Cellular Automata. The existing panels and texture-reading excerpts are supplied; this reflective threshold does not require repairing the exhibit or claim that its missing feedback already works.
halls.storyboard_short: Use green panel and apparently grown frost. Reuse retained form, Paint history and old/new state. Trace inputs; name what a changed mark must leave for next update. Check: explain clock restart versus state restore. Carry old-state → rule → new-state contract into CA. Supply panels/texture-reading excerpts. Host lacks previous-frame feedback; no promise of evolving chemistry or implemented transport.
learns: feedback requires a retained, connected input
halls.carries: An explicit old-state → rule → new-state contract for Cellular Automata
halls.review_note: The host does not bind the previous-frame texture. Preserve this honest threshold. The Book of Shaders contents lists simulation topics, but the linked chapters used here do not supply a finished Godot reaction-diffusion lesson.
halls.independent_check: Explain why restarting TIME can reproduce a coordinate-driven image but does not restore the history of a stateful simulation. Name the missing input in the existing panel.
halls.critical_question: What history can this appearance justify claiming?

status: Revised teaching proposal; not expanded lessons or implemented learner adapters

arc: PROPOSED. Give a local rule a stored present and a separate next state, then inspect history, neighbourhoods, graded values and bodily inputs. Follow the actual artifacts rather than the historical hall names: ElementaryRules contains a three-state volume, GameOfLife a one-dimensional history bridge, and BeyondBinary a binary Life dish. Recursion is previewed by comparison and taught in the following sequence.

halls.title: Build the next row from the held row
halls.storyboard: At the held rule explorer, the student predicts the marked cell before pressing STEP and finds the same history overhead. Bringing lists, loops, conditions and Shaders' missing-memory question, they construct a row update that reads three old values, writes one next value, and swaps arrays only after every address is processed. The row display, controls and wrapped-ring receiver are supplied. They learn synchronous local updates and make the boundary rule explicit. The reusable result is a small cellular engine whose stored history can be displayed without confusing it with the current row.
halls.storyboard_short: Use held rule explorer and overhead history. Reuse lists, loops, conditions and Shaders' old/new-state contract. Teach reading three old values to write one next value; swap arrays after completing the row. Predict one cell; declare boundaries. Supply display, controls and wrapped-ring receiver. Carry synchronous engine with separate history. Open: choose readable rule table before bit encoding; rug symmetry is separate.
halls.carries: A row update with explicit boundary handling
halls.review_note: Choose a readable rule table before using bit encoding; the rug's symmetry is a separate operation.

halls.title: Give a cell a fading state
halls.storyboard: The small volume and enlarged twenty-seven-position neighbourhood reveal active, fading and empty cells. Bringing synchronous updates and multidimensional addresses, the student constructs a three-state transition function, then traces one actual neighbourhood through a supplied counter. An active cell can cease participating while its fading state remains visible. The volume renderer, enlarged witness and twenty-six-neighbour enumerator are supplied with their contracts. They leave able to separate a state's persistence from its displayed colour and to reuse a transition table, while recognizing that rendered, occupied and active counts can answer different questions.
halls.storyboard_short: Use active/fading/empty volume and enlarged neighbourhood. Reuse synchronous updates and multidimensional addresses. Teach three-state transition table; trace one count through the supplied twenty-six-neighbour enumerator. Supply renderer and witness. Carry state transitions separate from colour; inactive fading cells can remain visible, so rendered, occupied and active counts differ. Follow the installed 3D study despite its historical title.
halls.carries: A three-state rule separate from state presentation
halls.review_note: The historical title is misleading; this hall currently owns a three-state 3D study, not another introductory elementary-row lesson.

halls.title: Turn recorded time into a structure
halls.storyboard: The desk, stepping tiles and ornamental screen receive one Rule 30 history. Bringing the row engine, copied snapshots and state-to-colour mapping, the student copies each completed row into a retained history, then constructs two receivers: one arranges generations across a flat drawing, the other passes occupied entries to a supplied piece placement interface. The desk, collision tiles and screen geometry are supplied. They gain a reusable history-to-space mapping and compare zero as no mark with zero as no support. Selecting an earlier row changes attention without rerunning the automaton or altering its stored past.
halls.storyboard_short: Use Rule 30 desk, stepping tiles and screen. Reuse row engine, copied snapshots and colour mapping. Teach retained history with flat-image and piece-placement receivers; select earlier rows without rerunning. Supply desk, collision tiles, screen and placement interface. Carry history-to-space mapping; zero may mean no mark or no support. Open: learner connection remains proposed; actual Life follows in CA_BeyondBinary.
halls.carries: A stored history with explicit spatial receivers
halls.review_note: The current primary is a one-dimensional Rule 30 history; actual Life follows in CA_BeyondBinary. The learner receiver connection is proposed.

halls.title: Let a fixed address control another object
halls.storyboard: At the Life dish, a glider crosses fixed gold addresses while lamps answer their occupancy. Bringing arrays, neighbour rules and explicit receivers, the student implements the small birth-and-survival decision from a supplied eight-neighbour count, then connects one retained cell reference to a lamp through a declared output function. The dish, floor image and lamp objects are supplied. They learn to distinguish a moving pattern from moving cells and leave with a usable simulation-to-object connection. The floor remains solid when its colour is empty, and the lamp sends no feedback into Life.
halls.storyboard_short: Use binary Life dish, fixed gold addresses and lamps. Reuse arrays, neighbour rules and receivers. Teach birth/survival from a supplied count with eight addresses explained; connect one fixed cell reference to lamp output. Supply dish, floor image and lamps. Carry state-to-object connection; patterns move across fixed cells, empty colour leaves solid floor, and lamps provide no feedback.
halls.carries: A local simulation state connected to a named object
halls.review_note: This installed study remains binary despite the map ID; keep the count helper explicit and introduce its eight addresses.

halls.title: Make the observing body an input
halls.storyboard: The bridge loses health near a probe or visitor, and its wall frieze shows the same values. Bringing synchronous arrays, distance and explicit outputs, the student constructs a local input function that turns a supplied position into a bounded health change at nearby cells. A separate neighbour rule restores health before colour and support read it. The player-position interface, bridge renderer and collision thresholds are supplied. They gain an input-update-output pattern and compare shared-old-state updates with in-place changes, discovering why scan order can alter the result before declaring the system responsive.
halls.storyboard_short: Use decaying bridge and matching frieze; choose probe for repeatability. Reuse synchronous arrays, distances and outputs. Teach bounded health changes near supplied positions; separate neighbour recovery from colour/support receivers. Compare shared-old-state and in-place updates to expose scan order. Supply position interface, bridge renderer and collision thresholds. Carry body-to-field input; keep player tracking supplied.
halls.carries: A bounded body-to-field input function
halls.review_note: Use the probe for repeatable comparisons; no need to teach the entire player tracking system.

halls.title: Exchange differences between neighbours
halls.storyboard: The matched concentration fields begin alike, but only one can pass its second substance across the seeded edge. Bringing graded state and synchronous buffers, the student constructs a small neighbour-difference sum and combines it with a supplied local reaction function. They track two concentration values at one witness before interpreting the resulting texture. The field displays, reaction function and one-time body-triggered seed are supplied. They learn how diffusion differs from counting occupied neighbours and carry a reusable two-field update, while the table and curved wall remain two receivers of the same state.
halls.storyboard_short: Use matched concentration fields. Reuse graded state and synchronous buffers. Teach neighbour-difference sums combined with supplied local reaction; track two concentrations at one witness before interpreting texture. Supply displays, Gray-Scott reaction and one-time body seed. Carry exchange separate from reaction; diffusion differs from occupied-neighbour counts. Table and curved wall share state. Defer reaction equations to Soft Bodies.
halls.carries: A two-field update with exchange separated from reaction
halls.review_note: Gray–Scott equations are supplied here and deepened in Soft Bodies; current artifacts supersede the sequence's older primary list.

halls.title: Compare resemblance with procedure
halls.storyboard: The Rule 90 history makes triangular gaps that resemble the nearby Sierpinski pyramid. Bringing the row engine and its stored history, the student creates two short procedural accounts: how one cell is calculated, and how the supplied pyramid copies smaller pieces. They vary the explorer's seed while keeping the pyramid fixed, recording which resemblances survive. The explorer, enlarged floor history and pyramid are supplied. No circuit or new syntax is required. They carry a precise question into Fractals: what is repeated, what information each step needs, and when a shared appearance conceals different work.
halls.storyboard_short: Use Rule 90 history and Sierpinski pyramid. Reuse row engine and retained history. Describe cell calculation versus copying smaller pieces; vary the row seed while holding the pyramid fixed. Supply explorer, enlarged floor history and pyramid. Carry procedural questions into Fractals without new syntax. Preserve resemblance as inquiry; Wireworld is an older proposal, not an installed circuit.
halls.carries: Two distinct accounts of a similar pattern
halls.review_note: Wireworld exists only as an older proposal here; do not teach an installed circuit that the current hall does not contain.

halls.title: Follow one deliberate difference
halls.storyboard: The two volumes begin with a single altered address, which a selected slice can reveal or hide. Bringing multidimensional arrays, synchronous updates and matched comparisons, the student makes a paired-state experiment: copy a beginning, change one value, run the same update, and record both the largest difference and how many sites differ. The volume solver, slice displays and body-selected depth interface are supplied. They leave with a reusable perturbation study that distinguishes spread from magnitude. Integer storage and display gain become inspectable choices, without promoting an attractive image into proof of a universal critical point.
halls.storyboard_short: Use paired volumes and selected slices. Reuse arrays, synchronous updates and matched comparisons. Teach copied beginnings with one altered value; run identical updates and forcing schedules, recording maximum difference and differing-site count. Supply solver, slices and body-selected depth. Carry magnitude versus spread; inspect integer storage and display gain. Claim no universal critical threshold from the image.
halls.carries: A paired experiment with separate extent and magnitude records
halls.review_note: The teaching comparison must use the same forcing schedule on both copies; no universal edge-of-chaos threshold is claimed.

arc: PROPOSED. Functions and loops already belong to the learner; self-calls and their stopping conditions are new. Develop repeated construction through branches, retained intervals, replacement segments and subdivided volumes. Use finite budgets honestly, then distinguish numerical recurrence from the geometry used to display it. The closing comparison prepares symbolic rewriting without pretending every recursive-looking artifact uses recursion.

halls.title: Let a function ask for a smaller task
halls.storyboard: At the nested-square desk and its floor-standing doorframes, the student asks for another term and encounters two different limits: depth and size. Bringing functions, scale and geometric construction, they write a small function that creates one square, then calls itself with reduced size and remaining depth. The line renderer, layout comparison and doorframe receiver are supplied. They can trace when each call stops and compare one descendant with several. The reusable outcome is bounded recursion, with its work budget distinguished from what an eye can resolve or a body can pass through.
halls.storyboard_short: Use nested-square desk and doorframes. Reuse functions, scale and geometry. Teach self-calls reducing size and remaining depth; trace base cases and compare one descendant with several. Supply lines, layout comparison and doorframe receiver. Carry bounded recursion; distinguish work budget, visual resolution and bodily clearance. Keep the actual square rule; branching rings may form a separate lesson.
halls.carries: A bounded recursive constructor
halls.review_note: Use the actual nested-square rule rather than an unrelated factorial example; branching rings can be a second short lesson.

halls.title: Pass a branch its starting state
halls.storyboard: The unfinished trunk gains children at its endpoint, and the enlarged canopy gives those connections bodily scale. Bringing bounded recursion, vectors and rotations, the student constructs a branch record with position, direction and length, then uses it to generate two child segments. The segment renderer, generation controls and canopy collision are supplied. They can change inherited length without changing branch count, or change descendants without merely widening the silhouette. They carry a reusable branching constructor, while comparing its recursive description with the installed tree's generation queue and keeping biological growth claims outside the rule.
halls.storyboard_short: Use unfinished trunk and enlarged canopy. Reuse bounded recursion, vectors and rotations. Teach branch records with position, direction and length; generate two children and vary inherited length separately from count. Supply segments, generation controls and collision. Carry explicit parent/child construction. Mark the recursive teaching version as proposed comparison: the installed tree uses a generation queue, without biological growth claims.
halls.carries: A branching constructor with explicit parent and child records
halls.review_note: The installed growing tree evaluates a generation queue; label the recursive teaching version as a proposed comparison, not its exact implementation.

halls.title: Keep intervals while removing their middles
halls.storyboard: At the stepped Cantor bars, the student sees more pieces but less retained length; the pagoda gives the gaps depth. Bringing lists, interval endpoints and bounded repetition, they construct the next interval list by keeping the first and last thirds of every current interval. They store the old rows separately so hiding history cannot remove more of the current set. The bar renderer, counters and collidable pagoda are supplied. The reusable outcome is a replacement operation with an explicit complement, and a finite construction that remains distinct from its mathematical limit.
halls.storyboard_short: Use stepped bars and pagoda. Reuse lists, endpoints and bounded repetition. Teach retaining first and last thirds into a new interval list; keep history separate. Compare increasing piece count with decreasing retained length. Supply bars, counters and collision. Carry finite replacement and complement; hiding old rows leaves the current set unchanged. Distinguish construction from limit. Open: endpoint pairs or centre/length records.
halls.carries: A finite interval generator and separate history
halls.review_note: Choose whether endpoint pairs or centre-and-length records give the clearest continuity with earlier geometry.

halls.title: Replace a segment with a detour
halls.storyboard: At the Koch desk, fixed endpoints enclose an increasingly long route; the Sierpinski study removes centres from faces. Bringing vector geometry, triangle corners and separate next lists, the student constructs one Koch replacement from a segment's endpoints, then applies it to every retained segment. The line renderer, step controls and comparison triangle are supplied. They measure endpoint distance separately from path length and carry a reusable geometry-replacement function. Sierpinski provides a second reading of replacement through midpoint faces; box-counting remains an optional measurement study rather than a prerequisite for making the curve.
halls.storyboard_short: Use Koch desk and Sierpinski comparison. Reuse vectors, triangle corners and separate next lists. Teach equilateral segment replacement across retained segments; measure endpoint distance separately from route length. Supply lines, steps and comparison triangle. Carry segment-to-segments transformation; inspect midpoint-face replacement separately. Defer optional box counting. Keep this rule distinct from the later five-segment right-angle L-system preset.
halls.carries: A segment-to-segments transformation
halls.review_note: Keep the equilateral Koch rule distinct from the later L-system editor's five-segment right-angle preset.

halls.title: Make removal create a passage
halls.storyboard: The nine-metre cube first offers no entrance, then reveals intersecting openings. Bringing three-dimensional addresses, scale and recursive replacement, the student writes a selection rule over a three-by-three-by-three block that retains twenty cells, then repeats it for a bounded number of levels. The block renderer, collision bodies and flight enclosure are supplied. They keep the original bounds while computing the changing retained volume and inspect the removed cells as another subject. The reusable outcome is a volume-subdivision rule whose connected holes still need testing against the size and abilities of a visitor.
halls.storyboard_short: Use the cube's opening passages. Reuse 3D addresses, scale and recursive replacement. Teach retaining twenty cells from a 3-by-3-by-3 block across bounded levels; compute retained volume within fixed bounds and inspect the complement. Supply blocks, collision and flight enclosure. Carry subdivision; test holes against visitor size/abilities. Preserve the existing restriction on rebuilding while occupied.
halls.carries: A finite retained-cell recipe and its complement
halls.review_note: Keep geometry changes outside an occupied structure; the current desk already restricts rebuilding while visitors inhabit it.

halls.title: Separate a recurrence from its drawing
halls.storyboard: The numbered towers grow by adding the previous pair, yet their displayed heights do not initially preserve those sums. Bringing arrays, accumulation and value mappings, the student makes a finite Fibonacci record and renders it with two explicit height functions, then checks a fixed-unit addition witness. The tower display, logarithm function and rectangle-cutting study are supplied. They gain a reusable distinction between numerical recurrence and geometric representation. The neighbouring rectangle and circular arcs leave room to ask which further choices produce a spiral, without treating resemblance in natural forms as evidence of one universal recipe.
halls.storyboard_short: Use numbered towers, addition witness and rectangle study. Reuse arrays, accumulation and mappings. Teach finite Fibonacci recurrence with two height mappings; compare displayed heights against fixed-unit sums. Supply tower display, logarithm input/output and rectangle construction. Carry numbers separate from representation. Ask what further choices create spiral arcs; claim no universal natural recipe. Defer optional logarithm derivation.
halls.carries: A numerical record with interchangeable mappings
halls.review_note: Do not introduce logarithms silently: supply their input-output mapping here, with a deeper derivation optional.

halls.title: Describe what repeats without naming the form
halls.storyboard: At the Cantor desk and fixed block tree, the student explains one construction without using its title. They bring replacement functions, parent records and explicit stopping rules, then make a compact recipe stating the input, descendants, placement and budget. Another student, or their own later reading, should be able to predict the next step from that account. The interval display, tree and history controls are supplied. No new syntax is needed. They carry a precise description of repeated work into L-systems, while separating a change to the construction from merely hiding its record.
halls.storyboard_short: Use Cantor desk and fixed block tree. Reuse replacement functions, parent records and stopping rules. Describe input, descendants, placement and budget without naming the form; predict the next step. Supply intervals, tree and history controls. Carry a precise recipe into L-systems; hiding records differs from changing construction. Require no new syntax. Defer editable cross-procedure comparison as future work.
halls.carries: A recipe precise enough to predict one next step
halls.review_note: An editable cross-procedure comparison is future work; the current hall supports describing and reading existing constructions.

arc: PROPOSED. Move from replacing geometry to rewriting symbols, then separate the sentence from the interpreter that gives it a body. Introduce an explicit stack for branching, develop footprints and conditional growth, and inspect the limits of parameter and shape vocabularies. Preserve the existing specimens; editable learner recipes and their transfer between the editor, turtle and construction studies remain proposed connections.

halls.title: Write a sentence before drawing it
halls.storyboard: The editor holds one drawing while the live version reads the same symbols with another turn angle. Bringing lists, traversal and geometric replacement, the student constructs one rewriting pass that reads an old string and appends each replacement to a new string. A supplied turtle interpreter draws the result, with its command meanings stated. The editor display and held witness are supplied. They can change a production separately from its interpretation and carry a usable symbolic generator, including the possibility that an undrawn symbol still participates in later rewriting.
halls.storyboard_short: Use held/live editor drawings. Reuse lists, traversal and geometric replacement. Teach one rewriting pass from old string to new; vary production separately from turn angle. Supply turtle with stated commands, display and witness. Carry symbolic generator and interpreter contract; undrawn symbols may rewrite later. Open: visitor-authored productions are not exposed; the learner-editable connection remains proposed.
halls.carries: A production rule and a separate interpreter contract
halls.review_note: Visitor-authored productions are not currently exposed; the learner-editable rule connection must be implemented after approval.

halls.title: Save a state and return to it
halls.storyboard: The parametric tree steps through a bracket without drawing, then returns to an earlier position and length. Bringing rewriting, directions and copied snapshots, the student constructs a stack of turtle states: push saves a copy of position, orientation and length; pop restores it. Command dispatch for drawing and turning remains supplied, alongside the sentence and rendered stepping witness. They attach their save-and-restore functions to the bracket commands, gaining reusable branching state without rebuilding the whole interpreter. Branch nesting differs from rewriting generation, and returning restores only what the saved record contains.
halls.storyboard_short: Use parametric tree's bracket steps. Reuse rewriting, directions and copied snapshots. Teach a stack: push copies position, orientation and length; pop restores them. Supply sentence, stepping witness and ordinary draw/turn dispatch. Carry explicit branching state; nesting differs from rewriting generations, and restoration covers only saved fields. Open: learner bracket handlers' connection to the interpreter remains proposed.
halls.carries: A turtle stack with an explicit state record
halls.review_note: Keep ordinary command dispatch supplied. The learner owns bracket handlers and copied state records; their connection to the existing interpreter is proposed.

halls.title: Change what forward means
halls.storyboard: The believing turtle keeps its gold heading while a blue reader draws sideways. Bringing the saved-state interpreter and transformations, the student writes a small interpretation function that converts the stored heading into a displacement, then compares direct and reflected readings of one sentence. The synchronized readers, arrow witnesses and tube-painting receiver are supplied. They gain a reusable interpreter variation while measuring what remains unchanged in segment lengths and connections. Turning the resulting trace into a tube can remain a later application; the unusual silhouette alone does not create different branch connectivity.
halls.storyboard_short: Use gold-heading turtle and sideways blue reader. Reuse saved state and transforms. Teach replaceable heading-to-displacement interpretation; compare direct/reflected readings of one sentence and check segment lengths/connectivity. Supply synchronized readers, arrows and tube receiver. Carry interpreter variation; changed silhouette need not change branching. Open: transferring learner trace into tube_painting is proposed; current controls change ring sides on supplied geometry.
halls.carries: A replaceable heading-to-displacement function
halls.review_note: Carrying the learner's trace into tube_painting is proposed; its installed lesson currently changes the ring side count on supplied geometry.

halls.title: Give a centreline a usable width
halls.storyboard: The dungeon begins as four pale centrelines, then BUILD raises a boundary a visitor can enter. Bringing turtle segments, offsets and collision distinctions, the student constructs a small footprint from a short orthogonal path, explicitly choosing corridor width and open ends. The wall builder, junction handling and collision assembly are supplied with their inputs stated. They can test whether a connected line becomes a usable passage for the prepared body. The reusable result is a path-to-footprint operation, while duplicate room records remain distinguishable from new physical rooms or meaningful uses.
halls.storyboard_short: Use dungeon centrelines and BUILD. Reuse turtle segments, offsets and collision distinctions. Teach an orthogonal path-to-footprint rule with stated width and open ends; test bodily passage. Supply wall builder, junction handling and collision with explicit inputs. Carry usable corridor footprints; duplicate room records need not create distinct rooms or uses. Defer arbitrary-angle joins and editable grammars.
halls.carries: A small corridor footprint with explicit openings
halls.review_note: Keep the first construction orthogonal; arbitrary-angle joining and new editable grammars are future work.

halls.title: Let a shared resource condition a rule
halls.storyboard: The amber and blue stems share a grammar, but reversing their first turns reverses the initial advantage. Bringing state updates, rewriting and stored resources, the student makes a small scheduling experiment in which two growth requests consult and consume the same resource record. The forest kernel, soil display and specimen renderer are supplied. They record the state before each request rather than explaining unequal results through different branch instructions. The reusable outcome is an explicit rule for conditional execution and turn order, with a possible shared-snapshot comparison marked as a new experiment.
halls.storyboard_short: Use amber/blue stems sharing one grammar. Reuse rewriting, updates and resources. Teach two requests consulting/consuming one mutable record; record state before each and reverse turn order. Supply forest kernel, soil display and specimens. Carry conditional execution and explicit schedule; unequal outcomes need not mean unequal instructions. Open: shared-snapshot comparison is a new experiment; claim no ecological equilibrium.
halls.carries: A visible schedule of requests and resource changes
halls.review_note: Do not claim ecological equilibrium; simultaneous shared-snapshot consumption is proposed, not an existing control.

halls.title: Map a design record into a body
halls.storyboard: Beside the held tree, several small Depth changes leave the branch plan unchanged before one crosses a rounding threshold. Bringing parameter records, rewriting and numeric mappings, the student constructs an explicit conversion from a short design record into bounded generation, angle and fork values, then retains the record used by a planted specimen. The tree builder, held witness and local planting interface are supplied. They leave with a reproducible design description and can identify requested changes with no address in it. The data's name, DNA, does not make the construction a biological simulation.
halls.storyboard_short: Use held tree's Depth rounding steps. Reuse parameter records, rewriting and mappings. Teach bounded generation, angle and fork conversion; retain the design record for a planted specimen. Supply builder, witness and local planting interface. Carry reproducible design with visible vocabulary limits; DNA naming does not establish biology. Open: distinguish local specimens from DNA export; cross-hall transport remains proposed.
halls.carries: A saved design record and its generated specimen
halls.review_note: Keep local planted specimens distinct from DNA export; cross-hall transport of either requires a new connection.

halls.title: Choose which part an operation can address
halls.storyboard: The six cube specimens reveal how an old diagonal makes two triangles available to inset and extrude; the later strip canopy gives one face another scale. Bringing face lists, transformations and saved configurations, the student specifies a small operation sequence on selected face indices and predicts its resulting connections. The inset, extrusion and curved-strip builders are supplied with named inputs and outputs; the fixed specimens provide comparisons. They gain a reusable shape recipe, and can tell when a desired form needs a new operation rather than another amount on an existing control.
halls.storyboard_short: Use fixed cubes and strip canopy. Reuse face lists, transforms and saved configurations. Specify selected face indices and an inset/extrusion sequence; predict resulting connections and inspect the inherited diagonal. Supply builders with explicit inputs/outputs, including curved strips. Carry a shape recipe; some desired forms require new operations. Open: editable learner recipe and preview remain proposed.
halls.carries: A shape recipe with explicit face selection
halls.review_note: The museum specimens are fixed. An editable learner recipe and preview are proposed, not existing controls.

halls.title: Give a retained choice another alphabet
halls.storyboard: The textile keeps the same 144 samples while diagonals become bars and then blocks. Bringing retained draws, thresholds and the separation of sentence from interpreter, the student constructs two mark dictionaries for one binary decision list and compares the paths they see in each rendering. The textile display, held witness and full-size floor receiver are supplied. They leave with a reusable separation of sample, decision and mark. This closes the sequence without requiring new syntax: a route perceived in an image need not have been requested, checked or made collidable by its generator.
halls.storyboard_short: Use textile's retained 144 samples. Reuse draws, thresholds and interpreter separation. Teach two mark dictionaries for one binary decision list; compare apparent paths as diagonals become bars or blocks. Supply textile, witness and floor receiver. Carry sample/decision/mark separation without new syntax; perceived routes need not be checked or collidable. Open: sharing the earlier generator's record remains proposed.
halls.carries: One retained decision list with several interpretations
halls.review_note: A mark dictionary can use the learner's earlier two-mark generator; sharing its actual record across halls is proposed.

arc: PROPOSED. Combine the already learned generators into scored selection, directed growth, connectivity, carving and sampling. Teach each new operation through a short construction with named supplied machinery. Do not assume the optional graph-theory branch was completed: any local search, adjacency list or traversal needed here must be introduced briefly or supplied explicitly, with full graph treatment reserved for the later spine sequence.

halls.title: Make a criterion explicit before selecting
halls.storyboard: The six boxes keep their descriptions while TARGET changes which one leads. Bringing design records, lists and measurement, the student writes a small evaluator that turns a candidate description into a declared score, then ranks a retained population without rebuilding it. The primitive builder, displayed candidates and reproduction kernel are supplied. They learn that generation, representation and evaluation are separate operations and can inspect which features their criterion ignores. The reusable outcome is an explicit selection procedure, while the held numerical leader need not be the body the student personally wanted to keep.
halls.storyboard_short: Use six boxes under changing TARGET. Reuse design records, lists and measurement. Teach explicit candidate scoring and ranking without rebuilding the population; inspect ignored features and compare the leader with personal preference. Supply primitive builder, display and reproduction kernel. Carry generation/evaluation separation. Use the approximate estimator honestly; exact union volume and learner-selected witness retention are not installed.
halls.carries: A declared candidate evaluator and ranked record
halls.review_note: Use the current approximate estimator honestly; exact union volume and learner-selected witness retention are not installed capabilities.

halls.title: Combine requests into a growth direction
halls.storyboard: Three attraction points ask the root to grow, and their sideways contributions cancel in its first proposed step. Bringing vector subtraction, normalization and branch records, the student constructs a direction accumulator from a supplied list of assigned points, then adds a fixed-length child segment. The attraction display, nearest-site assignment and segment renderer are supplied. They gain a reusable way to combine unit directions, while comparing which sites remain eligible to respond in later generations. These points are consulted coordinates, so the resulting growth should not be described as simulated forces or light-seeking biology.
halls.storyboard_short: Use three attraction points and cancelling sideways requests. Reuse vector operations and branch records. Teach summing assigned unit directions into a fixed-length child step; compare later site eligibility. Supply attraction display, nearest-site assignment and segment renderer. Carry a request-driven branch rule; consulted coordinates are not simulated forces or light-seeking biology. Defer nearest-site search to a separate follow-up.
halls.carries: A fixed-step branch rule driven by assigned requests
halls.review_note: Nearest-site assignment is supplied initially; its search can be a separate short follow-up.

halls.title: Choose one request and keep its provenance
halls.storyboard: The branch leans towards its nearest attraction point instead of combining every invitation. Bringing the previous direction accumulator and distance comparisons, the student constructs a nearest-eligible-point search, retains the chosen point's index, and makes one fixed-length child step. The attraction layout, branch renderer and stepped clock are supplied. Recording both parent and target lets them explain coincident children before adding jitter or a pulsing length. They carry a reusable selection-and-growth operation, distinguishing the number of records from the number of distinct positions visible in the resulting structure.
halls.storyboard_short: Use nearest-attraction branching. Reuse direction accumulation and distance comparisons. Teach nearest-eligible search; retain parent and target index before making a fixed-length step. Supply attraction layout, renderer and stepped clock. Carry growth provenance; explain coincident children before jitter or pulsing, distinguishing record count from distinct positions. Open: shared attraction concepts exist, but transferring the learner's record remains proposed.
halls.carries: A branch record naming its parent and selected target
halls.review_note: Shared attraction data across the two halls is conceptually established; transferring the learner's own record remains proposed.

halls.title: Declare which contacts transmit
halls.storyboard: Two cubes touch at a face, then at a corner; only one arrangement passes flow in the study's rule. Bringing grid neighbours, occupancy and synchronous updates, the student constructs a six-neighbour transmission step for a small retained volume. They keep random occupancy generation separate from flow state so the same lattice can be tested from another source. The cube display, source fixture and stepping controls are supplied. They carry a reusable local propagation operation and understand that a visible contact, a permitted adjacency and a globally reachable path are different claims.
halls.storyboard_short: Use face-touching versus corner-touching cubes. Reuse grid neighbours, occupancy and synchronous updates. Teach six-neighbour transmission with flow state separate from random occupancy; retest the retained lattice from another source. Supply cube display, source and stepping. Carry local propagation; distinguish visible contact, permitted adjacency and global reachability. Infer no universal threshold from one finite seeded lattice.
halls.carries: A propagation rule separate from the occupancy field
halls.review_note: Do not infer a universal percolation threshold from one finite seeded lattice.

halls.title: Carve enough room around a route
halls.storyboard: The cave's gold dots identify carving centres, while the neighbouring maze reveals a different route-making procedure. Bringing the random walk, grid addresses and occupancy, the student makes a carving function that clears a stated footprint and headroom around each retained centre. The cave renderer, collision builder and maze backtracking demonstration are supplied. They can keep the same centres while changing clearance and inspect what the record omitted. The reusable outcome is a path-to-empty-volume operation; separate walkers' dots must not be joined into a fictitious continuous trail, and an opening still needs a bodily test.
halls.storyboard_short: Use cave carving dots and maze comparison. Reuse walks, grid addresses and occupancy. Teach clearing footprint and headroom around retained centres; vary clearance, then test bodily access. Supply cave renderer, collision builder and backtracking demonstration. Carry path-to-empty-volume construction; never join separate walkers' dots into a fictitious trail. Defer optional maze implementation; introduce visited record and stack if chosen.
halls.carries: A clearance-aware carving operation
halls.review_note: A full backtracking maze implementation is optional; if selected later, introduce its visited record and stack explicitly.

halls.title: Make a surface from a chosen sample
halls.storyboard: Twelve falling cubes become a frozen centre record and then a blocky surface. Bringing coordinate frames, voxel addresses and mesh faces, the student makes a small sampler that converts body centres into the artifact's local frame, marks a declared neighbourhood, and submits exposed faces to a supplied mesh assembler. The falling bodies, sampling control and collision builder are supplied. They carry an event-to-surface pipeline whose omissions are visible: rotation and exact contact shapes were not recorded. The dome's cutting cores remain a comparison that prepares later Boolean work, rather than an unexplained prerequisite.
halls.storyboard_short: Use falling cubes becoming a frozen blocky surface. Reuse frames, voxel addresses and faces. Teach local-frame centre sampling, declared neighbourhood marking and exposed-face submission. Supply bodies, sampling control, mesh assembler and collision. Carry event-to-surface reconstruction with actual enlarged dimensions; rotation and contact shapes are omitted. Keep dome cuts as comparison; defer Boolean machinery.
halls.carries: A local-position sample with a declared reconstruction rule
halls.review_note: The existing neighbourhood enlarges each cube substantially; teach its actual dimensions, not an exact reconstruction claim.

halls.title: Copy an image and inspect a connection
halls.storyboard: The held cellular field acquires symmetry while the neighbouring network changes its connection policy. Bringing array addresses, transformations and retained inputs, the student constructs a reflection operator that reads one region and writes a separate result, then checks centre rows and columns explicitly. The field display, network comparison and tunnel surfaces are supplied. They leave with a reusable copying operation and two distinct accounts of repetition: repeated values in an image and repeated access between sites. The network remains an observation model, and formal graph measures can wait for their later sequence.
halls.storyboard_short: Use mirrored cellular field and network comparison. Reuse array addresses, transforms and retained inputs. Teach reading one region into a separate reflected result; check centre rows/columns. Supply field, network, tunnel surfaces and graph statistics. Carry explicit reflection boundaries; repeated image values differ from repeated access. Network collision is disabled. Defer formal graph measures; do not claim traversability.
halls.carries: A reflection operator with explicit boundary treatment
halls.review_note: Do not treat the current rhizomatic specimen as traversable; its collision is disabled. Supply graph statistics without assuming earlier graph coursework.

arc: PROPOSED. Reuse mesh connectivity, forces, state and constraints to distinguish a deformable body from an animated surface. Give the learner small constructions around supplied solvers: a mesh attachment, a pin selection, a driven boundary, a measured response and a frozen snapshot. Return to Gray–Scott with reaction and exchange separated. Isosurface extraction and Boolean operations come later in the spine, so their machinery stays supplied here.

halls.title: Give a connected mesh to a solver
halls.storyboard: The pinned jelly cube yields while retaining its face connections. Bringing meshes, forces and physical bodies, the student connects a supplied subdivided mesh to a soft-body solver, retains the body reference and pins one selected point. They compare resistance, damping and pressure by following the same deformation rather than treating all three as softness. The mesh generator, Godot solver and hand-contact rig are supplied. They leave with a reusable deformable-body setup and a precise account of its attachment, while recognizing that a tracked hand can displace the skin without being pushed back itself.
halls.storyboard_short: Use pinned jelly cube. Reuse mesh connectivity, forces and bodies. Teach attaching supplied subdivided mesh to solver, retaining its reference and pinning one point; compare resistance, damping and pressure on one deformation. Supply mesh generator, solver and hand-contact rig. Carry explicit deformable attachment; tracked hands need not receive reaction. Open: choose understandable vertex selection, not an unexplained index.
halls.carries: A connected deformable mesh with an explicit attachment
halls.review_note: Choose a reliable point-selection interface; do not bury mesh vertex selection behind an unexplained index.

halls.title: Choose the boundary that must stay
halls.storyboard: The hanging strips remain suspended when their gantry disappears, exposing a pin rule independent of visible support. Bringing mesh coordinates, conditions and the soft-body setup, the student constructs a vertex-selection function for an upper edge, then another for its corners, and applies the selected pins to a supplied open sheet. The cloth mesh, solver and support display are supplied. They gain a reusable boundary-condition recipe and can explain why an open surface has no enclosed volume to inflate. The tension membrane extends the comparison to a load acting between retained anchors.
halls.storyboard_short: Use hanging strips and tension membrane. Reuse coordinates, conditions and soft-body setup. Teach vertex-selection functions for upper edge versus corners on a supplied open sheet. Supply cloth, solver and support display; use known generated coordinates. Carry boundary-condition recipe; disappearing gantry does not remove pins, and an open surface encloses no inflatable volume. Compare loads between retained anchors.
halls.carries: A named vertex-selection rule for attachments
halls.review_note: The learner's reduced sheet should use known generated coordinates; keep decorative gantry changes separate from actual attachment.

halls.title: Drive an attachment while matter responds
halls.storyboard: At the revolving ride, the support stops commanding new angles while the hanging bodies continue moving. Bringing rotations, time steps and pinned or jointed constraints, the student writes a small driven-anchor rule with a rate in radians per second, then supplies that anchor to an existing hanging-body assembly. The hub, hinge connections and soft-body solver are supplied. They can stop or reverse the driver while retaining the body's state, gaining a reusable distinction between prescribed motion and simulated response. The attachment's one-way authority remains explicit: the hanging body cannot change the commanded hub rotation.
halls.storyboard_short: Use revolving ride. Reuse rotations, time steps and constraints. Teach an anchor driver in radians per second; stop or reverse it while retaining hanging-body state. Supply hub, hinges and solver. Carry prescribed motion versus simulated response; bodies cannot alter commanded hub rotation. Open: the reduced anchor connection remains proposed, with one-way authority explicit.
halls.carries: A time-based anchor driver with persistent downstream state
halls.review_note: The reduced anchor connection is proposed; do not imply the driven hub receives reaction forces from the hanging bodies.

halls.title: Use a wave as a force input
halls.storyboard: The breathing room's wall edges stay fixed while their centres respond to periodic pressure. Bringing sine, scalar receivers and pinned boundaries, the student constructs a pressure-driver function and connects its output to a supplied deformable panel. They hold the driver phase and observe that the solver can still settle under the retained pressure. The wall mesh, soft-body solver and museum support are supplied. They carry a reusable signal-to-force connection, distinguish it from directly displacing vertices, and test how a changing enclosure affects the clearance available to the prepared body.
halls.storyboard_short: Use breathing room's fixed wall edges. Reuse sine, scalar receivers and pinned boundaries. Teach a bounded panel's pressure driver; hold phase while the solver settles, then inspect bodily clearance. Supply wall mesh, solver and support. Carry signal-to-force input separate from solver state and direct vertex displacement. Open: connecting the learner's driver to both full walls needs an adapter.
halls.carries: A pressure driver separate from solver state
halls.review_note: Keep the first teaching panel bounded and inspectable; extending the learner's driver to both full walls needs an explicit adapter.

halls.title: Construct a comparison that earns its name
halls.storyboard: The twelve falling-body cells vary material, shape and contact in different combinations. Bringing solver settings, collision geometry and repeatable setup recipes, the student assembles a two-case comparison description that names every shared condition and one intended difference, using the High Drag case as an existing example. The gallery bodies, reset controls and physical solver are supplied. They record an observable consequence such as settling duration instead of relying on the case name. The reusable outcome is a controlled experiment recipe, with a seeded construction distinguished from a guarantee of identical physics across machines.
halls.storyboard_short: Use twelve falling-body cells and High Drag example. Reuse settings, collision geometry and repeatable setups. Teach a two-case comparison naming shared conditions and one changed factor; record a concrete consequence. Supply bodies, reset, solver and measurement support. Carry controlled experiment record; seeded construction does not guarantee identical cross-machine physics. Open: choose observable and supplied recorder.
halls.carries: A comparison record with shared and changed conditions
halls.review_note: Choose a concrete observable and a supplied way to record it; avoid making measurement infrastructure the lesson.

halls.title: Keep a result and name what was measured
halls.storyboard: The rounded body's volume display can feed back into pressure, while the glass vessel freezes a solver after a chosen step budget. Bringing retained positions, measurements and physical state, the student makes a snapshot operation that copies a supplied solver's current vertices into a static mesh while preserving face connections. The solver, vertex-reading interface and mesh assembler are supplied. They leave with a reusable process-to-sculpture operation and compare its loss of motion with the live instrument's bounding-box proxy. Freezing a closed surface does not cut the opening its vessel-like appearance may suggest.
halls.storyboard_short: Use volume-feedback body and frozen glass vessel. Reuse retained positions, faces and physical measurements. Teach copying current solver vertices into a static mesh with unchanged connectivity. Supply custom vessel solver's readable positions and mesh assembler; do not assume identical Godot access. Carry snapshot and conditions; compare lost motion with bounding-box volume proxy. Freezing closed geometry creates no opening.
halls.carries: A frozen mesh with its simulation conditions recorded
halls.review_note: Select the custom vessel solver's readable positions; do not assume Godot's soft-body vertices expose the identical interface.

halls.title: Keep recognition beside the recipe
halls.storyboard: The radiolaria row suggests shells, pollen and organisms before its six construction recipes are explained. Bringing primitives, seeded populations and shader effects, the student chooses two forms and makes an account of which cues produce that recognition, then tests one cue while retaining the construction seed. The geometric families, rotation controls and particle effects are supplied. No new syntax is required. They carry a more deliberate vocabulary for composing apparent life, while keeping a body's resemblance, its available interaction and the mechanism generating it as separate questions that may remain artistically unresolved.
halls.storyboard_short: Use radiolaria row. Reuse primitives, seeded populations and effects. Compare two forms' recognition cues; vary one while retaining the construction seed. Supply geometric families, rotation and particles. Carry deliberate apparent-life composition without new syntax; resemblance, interaction and mechanism remain separate, potentially unresolved questions. COLOUR rebuilds geometry, so pin a seed before treating it as palette-only.
halls.carries: A deliberate account of the cues used in a form
halls.review_note: COLOUR rebuilds geometry in this artifact; pin a seed before using it as a palette-only comparison.

halls.title: Separate reaction from exchange
halls.storyboard: A seeded patch changes across the held concentration grid, returning to the exchange study from Cellular Automata. Bringing two-field buffers, neighbour differences and small time steps, the student now constructs the local Gray–Scott reaction, feed and removal terms, then combines them with the known diffusion operation. The grid display, bounded stepping controls and initial field are supplied. They can hold one beginning while comparing update rules, or hold a rule while changing its seed pattern. The reusable outcome is a complete small field simulation, without claiming these are Turing's original equations or a biological organism.
halls.storyboard_short: Use held concentration grid. Reuse CA_SoftRules' two-field buffers, neighbour differences and time steps. Teach Gray-Scott reaction, feed and removal terms; combine with known diffusion. Supply display, stable stepping and initial field. Compare one beginning across rules or one rule across seeds. Carry complete update with separate contributions. Defer numerical limits; claim neither Turing's original equations nor an organism.
halls.carries: A complete two-concentration update with separated contributions
halls.review_note: CA_SoftRules supplies the reaction function first; this hall opens it. Use supplied stable step settings before exploring numerical limits.

halls.title: Expose the choices behind one gesture
halls.storyboard: The folded field surface changes several ways when S moves, while NOISE, LEVEL and RESOLUTION reveal separate interventions. Bringing sine fields, thresholds and composed mappings, the student makes an explicit control function that returns named frequency, noise and cut-level values instead of an unexplained master amount. The sampled-field generator, surface extractor and collision builder are supplied. They can compare one bundled gesture with independent choices and carry a reusable, inspectable control recipe. The source name entropy is not a measured distribution, and a visible opening remains a question of geometry and bodily clearance.
halls.storyboard_short: Use folded field with S, NOISE, LEVEL and RESOLUTION. Reuse sine fields, thresholds and mappings. Teach explicit control returning named frequency, noise and cut-level values; compare bundled gesture with independent choices. Supply field generator, surface extractor and collision. Carry inspectable controls; entropy is a source name, not a measurement, and openings need clearance tests. Defer extraction to Isosurfaces.
halls.carries: A control recipe whose component choices remain visible
halls.review_note: Surface extraction is supplied here because Isosurfaces follows at order 18; do not assume marching cubes was already taught.
